title: Winners named in Savannah Lively foundation photo contest
text:
The Savannah Lively Butterfly Legacy Inc. has announced the winners of its first photography contest, created to honor Savannah Lively and encourage other artists to share their work.
Kristi Meeks, a teacher from Monticello, won the amateur division with a photograph featuring rocks and water, a news release said, while Heaven Turner received the community choice award for a photograph of a stream surrounded by woods.
The photographs were featured during a juried art exhibition Sept. 4 at Emergent Arts, one day after what would have been Savannah Lively's birthday.
No entries were received in the professional or youth divisions, according to Jennifer Lively, Savannah's mother and a founder of the nonprofit.
Meeks donated her winnings back to the foundation.
"She was simply putting her work out there to see what would happen, which is exactly what we hoped to encourage in artists like Savannah," Jennifer Lively said in the release.
Savannah's parents, James and Jennifer Lively, formed the nonprofit after their daughter died in a car crash in August 2025.
Savannah had a longtime interest in photography but sometimes lacked confidence in sharing her work, Jennifer Lively previously told The Sentinel-Record. The family created the contest in part to encourage other artists to take that step.
The photography contest began April 1 and included professional, amateur and youth divisions. Money raised through the contest supports the foundation's scholarship efforts and planned outreach involving homeless veterans and stray animals, causes Jennifer Lively said were important to Savannah.
The foundation has already awarded a $500 scholarship to Bismarck High School graduate Cailsey Ellenwood, who planned to attend Henderson State University and study education.
Michael Goldman, Savannah's cousin and a member of the foundation, presented Turner with her award at the exhibition.
Jennifer Lively previously said she hopes the contest reminds artists not to wait to share their work.
"There's not always tomorrow," she said. "You don't always get another chance. Put it out there."
